title: Beatrix and the Confession
premise: Odile Sandoval, a concierge at the Hotel Verlaine with a gift for reading guests, is handed a diary belonging to Beatrix Vane, a guest who vanished eleven years ago and was declared dead. The diary's final entries are dated after her disappearance, written in a hand that isn't hers — someone has been keeping it alive, and someone wants Odile to find out why. Following the diary through the hotel's hidden rooms and the Vane family's poisoned inheritance, Odile discovers Beatrix faked her death to escape a controlling uncle who controlled the estate, and that an old porter has been secretly writing to her ever since as her found family. In the end, Odile closes the case by reuniting Beatrix with her chosen family rather than exposing her, letting the official record stay closed while the truth lives on in the diary's last true entry.
about_author: Casper Blackwood is the pen name of a former night-shift hotel worker who spent a decade listening to other people's secrets through lobby conversations. They write quiet mysteries about people who notice too much.

chapters.title: The Guest Who Never Checked Out
chapters.summary: Odile Sandoval, POV. While cataloguing items from the Verlaine's sealed long-term storage, Odile finds a diary belonging to Beatrix Vane, a guest who vanished in 2013. The final entry is dated three years after she disappeared. Emotional beat: professional curiosity curdling into unease as Odile realizes the case everyone closed was never finished.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile interviews retired staff about Beatrix: the uncle, Ambrose Vane, who visited weekly until his death; the young porter, Tomas, who wept at her memorial. Each account contradicts the others. Emotional beat: the slow realization that memory itself is unreliable testimony, and that everyone remembers the Beatrix they needed.

chapters.title: Entries in Another Hand
chapters.summary: Odile, POV, intercut with diary excerpts. Forensic comparison shows the post-disappearance entries were written by someone else — but with intimate knowledge of Beatrix's voice. The writer knew things only Beatrix could have told them. Emotional beat: intimacy without identity; Odile begins to feel they're reading a correspondence, not a record.

chapters.title: Room 407
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Behind Room 407's wardrobe, Odile finds a hidden panel and signs of long habitation: a cot, canned food, a second journal half-burned. Someone lived here after the disappearance — or Beatrix never left when they said she did. Emotional beat: dread; the hotel becomes a body with secrets in its walls.

chapters.title: The Vane Inheritance
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Digging into probate records, Odile learns Beatrix's disappearance made Ambrose sole heir to the hotel-owning trust — and that the Verlaine itself was the prize. A lawyer hints Ambrose feared Beatrix would return to contest it. Emotional beat: motive surfaces; the mystery sharpens from melancholy to menace.

chapters.title: Tomas Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Odile confronts Tomas, now the Verlaine's aging head porter, with the diary. He denies everything — too quickly, and his hands shake. That night Odile catches him burning papers in the boiler room. Emotional beat: betrayal; the gentlest witness may be the most guilty, or the most frightened.

chapters.title: What the Diary Kept Writing
chapters.summary: Odile, POV, with full diary excerpts. The post-disappearance entries describe Beatrix alive: a coastal town, a new name, letters home that were never sent. The writer wasn't forging her voice — they were answering letters she mailed in secret for years. Emotional beat: hope; Beatrix may be alive, and someone loved her enough to keep her voice breathing.

chapters.title: The Confession
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Tomas confesses: he helped Beatrix vanish to escape Ambrose, then wrote the diary entries from her letters so the hotel would remember her truly. But the letters stopped two years ago. Emotional beat: grief and tenderness; the confession reframes every lie as an act of loyalty, and opens a worse question — why did she stop writing?

chapters.title: Where the Letters Ended
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Tracing the letters' postmark, Odile travels to the coastal town and finds Beatrix elderly, unwell, and hiding not from Ambrose but from the shame of having abandoned Tomas to bear the secret alone. Climactic beat: confrontation and forgiveness; Beatrix must decide whether to be found, and Odile must decide what closing a case really means.

chapters.title: The Last True Entry
chapters.summary: Odile, POV. Beatrix returns quietly to the Verlaine, not as its heir but as a guest; Tomas meets her in the lobby after eleven years. Odile writes the diary's final entry in their own hand and seals the case file, leaving the official record untouched. Resolution beat: found family restored, inheritance renounced, memory honored — the one case closed by refusing to expose it.
